Trauma-informed by design

Understanding behaviour creates more opportunities to prevent harm.

Many incidents are connected to distress, fear, confusion, pain, intoxication, cognitive impairment or mental health crisis. That never excuses violence, but it changes how risk can be reduced.

We do not begin with “How do we control this?”
We begin with “What is happening for this person?”

The programme is not trauma therapy. Its contribution is practical: safer interactions, less escalation, reduced unnecessary physical intervention and more proportionate, defensible decisions.

Fear and uncertaintyHelping crews identify threat responses and reduce avoidable escalation.
Pain and distressKeeping communication clear when a person's capacity to cope is reduced.
Mental health crisisResponding with calm, structure and appropriate professional boundaries.
Confusion and dementiaAdapting pace, language and expectations to the person.
IntoxicationRecognising changing risk and maintaining safer distance and options.
Environmental pressureManaging risk in confined vehicles, homes, public places and unpredictable scenes.

Physical intervention remains important.
But it sits at the end of the process, not the beginning.

A complete learning pathway

From early prevention to safer intervention.

Organisations can select the modules that match their risk profile, workforce and clinical responsibilities, building a coherent pathway rather than a collection of disconnected courses.

Prevent

Introduction to Positive Approaches to Behaviour

Understand behaviour, recognise instinctive reactions and identify preventative measures that reduce risk.

Communicate

Introduction to De-escalation

Practical strategies for slowing situations down and communicating under pressure.

Protect

Personal Safety and Disengagement Skills

Safer, lawful options for protecting staff when prevention and de-escalation are no longer enough.

Guide

Guiding Skills

Supportive, proportionate skills for movement and cooperation while preserving dignity and choice wherever possible.

Intervene safely

Clinical Containment Skills

Specialist content for reducing the risks associated with restrictive interventions when essential clinical care cannot otherwise be delivered. The emphasis remains on necessity, proportionality, least restriction and harm reduction.

Real learning for real environments

Ambulance-specific scenarios, language and practical application.

The programme uses visual demonstrations and scenarios rooted in ambulance practice, from communication around a vehicle to patient movement, guiding and personal safety.

Where this approach was proven

Built and tested in ambulance services before it came to Australia.

Maybo was selected to support the AACE programme, helping develop a nationally consistent approach grounded in legality, proportionality and the realities of ambulance work. The programme was adopted by 11 of 14 UK Ambulance Trusts, providing a strong example of how a consistent behavioural safety approach can be embedded across ambulance services.

Where the ambulance handover meets the ED

Hear from emergency medicine.

Specialist video content connects practical behavioural safety with clinical realities, helping crews understand risk, patient vulnerability and the consequences of restrictive or pharmacological intervention. It supports the same consistent, trauma-informed handling QAS crews need at handover into Queensland Health emergency departments.

Dr Tony Bleetman
Consultant in Emergency Medicine
